content: Niemann-Pick disease, type C1 (NPC1), is a disorder caused by a defect in a membrane protein responsible for intracellular cholesterol trafficking in mammals. In humans, this protein is encoded by the NPC1 gene, which is located on chromosome 18q11. The NPC1 gene was identified as the gene that, when mutated, leads to Niemann-Pick disease, type C. This disease is a rare neurovisceral lipid storage disorder that arises from autosomal recessive loss-of-function mutations in either the NPC1 or NPC2 genes. These mutations disrupt intracellular lipid transport, resulting in the accumulation of lipid products within late endosomes and lysosomes. Approximately 95% of patients with Niemann-Pick disease, type C, have mutations in the NPC1 gene. The NPC1 protein is thought to be an integral membrane protein with sequence motifs that suggest a role in the intracellular transport of cholesterol to post-lysosomal destinations. Clinical Significance Obesity Mutations in the NPC1 gene have been strongly associated with obesity. A genome-wide association study identified NPC1 mutations as a risk factor for childhood obesity and adult morbid obesity. These mutations were also linked to ordinary weight gain in the general population. Studies in mice have suggested that the NPC1 gene plays a role in appetite regulation, as mice with a non-functioning NPC1 gene exhibit late-onset weight loss and reduced food intake. Variants in the NPC1 gene may account for approximately 10% of all childhood obesity cases and about 14% of adult morbid obesity cases. HIV-AIDS Cholesterol pathways are critical at multiple stages of the HIV-1 infection cycle. Processes such as HIV-1 fusion, entry, assembly, and budding occur at cholesterol-enriched microdomains known as lipid rafts. The HIV-1 accessory protein Nef has been shown to upregulate genes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis and homeostasis. Intracellular cholesterol trafficking pathways mediated by NPC1 are essential for efficient HIV-1 production. Ebola Virus The human NPC1 cholesterol transporter is crucial for Ebola virus infection. Multiple independent studies have demonstrated that the Ebola virus enters human cells by binding to NPC1. Laboratory experiments showed that cells from Niemann-Pick type C patients, which lack this transporter, were resistant to Ebola virus infection, indicating that the virus relies on NPC1 to enter cells. Similar findings were observed with the Marburg virus, another filovirus, which also requires NPC1 for cell entry. One study revealed that NPC1 mediates filovirus infection by directly binding to the viral envelope glycoprotein. A subsequent study confirmed that the second lysosomal domain of NPC1 is responsible for this binding. In one of the original studies, a small molecule was shown to inhibit Ebola virus infection by preventing the viral glycoprotein from binding to NPC1. Another study demonstrated that mice heterozygous for NPC1 were protected from lethal challenge with mouse-adapted Ebola virus. Collectively, these findings suggest that NPC1 could be a potential therapeutic target for developing antiviral drugs against Ebola. Mechanisms in Pathology In a mouse model carrying the underlying mutation for Niemann-Pick type C1 disease in the NPC1 protein, the expression of Myelin gene Regulatory Factor (MRF) was found to be significantly reduced. MRF is a transcription factor critical for the development and maintenance of myelin sheaths. Disruption in oligodendrocyte maturation and the myelination process may therefore represent an underlying mechanism contributing to the neurological deficits observed in this disease.
